title: I Ate a Special Chocolate that Changed My Appetite
description: For three separate weeks, I started every lunch with a bar of chocolate. Same ritual, every single day. The bars looked identical. They tasted identical. I couldn’t tell them apart. But during one stretch of that experiment, I ended up eating about 500 extra Calories at lunch, day after day, without ever feeling like I was overeating. Same chocolate. Same taste. 500 more Calories. So, what was going on? Today I’m going to explain science that might change how you eat sweets forever. A Sweet Molecule Is Not Just a Sweet Molecule Now, I should reveal that these weren’t just chocolate bars I picked off the shelf. I made them from scratch, and the difference between them was the sweetener I used. Because the fact of the matter is that different sweet molecules have different chemical structures. And even if there isn’t much difference on your tongue, your nervous system beyond your mouth can detect the difference. Different structures. Different receptors. Different downstream effects. But all beneath your conscious awareness. As a result, one sweet molecule may lead you to subconsciously eat more than another sweet molecule. At least that’s the theory. But now I should back up and explain the impetus for the experiment. It came from a paper published in Cell Metabolism that asked a simple question: How is sugar sensed by the nervous system in the gut? The advantage of using animals in this type of experiment is that you can do something a little sinister. Not only can you control calories by giving sugar alone, fat alone, or a calorie-matched combination of sugar and fat, but you can also bypass taste entirely by implanting small tubes that infuse those nutrients directly into the stomach or intestines. Then you can monitor how much the animals eat.

title: Does High HDL Cancel Out High ApoB?
description: Could good metabolic health make you immune to the dangers of high LDL and ApoB? Well, a new study published in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology just threw a wrench into the story that high LDL and ApoB are always bad. Don’t believe me? Here’s a quote: “When HDL-C is high, the effect of changing ApoB vanishes.” Not diminishes. “Vanishes.” And this study of nearly 300,000 people aligns with my own N=1. I have zero plaque (0 mm 3 ) in any of my arteries, soft or calcified, on advanced cardiac imaging, despite spending the better part of a decade with an LDL near 600 mg/dL and ApoB well over 300. Those are levels that would give your average cardiologist nightmares. So, what gives? Do I have “immunity” to the dangers of high ApoB, a word the authors themselves use? And, perhaps more importantly… what about you? Now, this might seem like a simple “woohoo” moment and victory lap for those with high HDL. But, like any good scientific story, there are a lot of nuances to unpack. But first, I want to introduce our characters and tell you what the researchers behind this study did. The Villain and the Hero: ApoB and HDL Our two big characters today are ApoB and HDL cholesterol (HDL-C). ApoB refers to a protein that sits on certain particles floating around in the bloodstream, collectively called the “ApoB-containing lipoproteins.” The most famous are the LDL particles. LDL particles are the key villain in the conventional cardiology story. And if you get a standard lipid panel and see an LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) value, that is the total cholesterol mass carried within your LDL particles. ApoB is considered a better risk marker than LDL cholesterol, since the amount of cholesterol in each particle can vary.

title: We Have Heart Disease Backwards (New Science)
description: “Our understanding of heart disease is completely backwards.” That was a text message sent to me by a physician colleague, accompanying the brand-new heart health paper we’re about to review. And it’s an opinion I hear more often than you might think. To give you a little insider knowledge, you’d be surprised how many credentialed MDs and PhDs privately express frustration with the dogmatism surrounding how we think about and manage cardiovascular disease. But you don’t need to take my word for it. Because the central issue is hiding in plain sight: we’ve become so narrowly focused on lowering LDL cholesterol and ApoB that we have missed some of the most important biology determining whether those biomarkers represent a true danger, or are more of a distraction. That doesn’t mean there’s zero truth to the conventional model of heart disease. But if you’re focused on a mosquito while a tiger is chasing you, the mosquito is still there. You’re just missing the bigger threat. And given that cardiovascular disease remains a leading killer, we should probably ask: What’s the proverbial tiger? Well, a new paper in a top science journal gives us a serious reason to reconsider whether our understanding of cardiovascular disease needs to be flipped on its head. This StayCurious Metabolism premium investigation is not for the faint of heart. We’re diving into groundbreaking research revealing a newly discovered “guardian of your arteries” and what happens when that protection fails.
